summary.text: Writing \(M=(2n+1)^2=2N+1\) with even \(N\), the carry identity \(a+b=(a\mathbin{\mathrm{XOR}}b)+2(a\mathbin{\mathrm{AND}}b)\) reduces the desired equation to \(k+(k^2\mathbin{\mathrm{AND}}M)=N\). Since adding \(2^i\) to \(k\) toggles the value of this left side by \(2^i\) modulo \(2^{i+1}\), one chooses \(k\)'s bits inductively modulo \(2^{M+1}\); elementary bounds leave either exact equality or a one-modulus overshoot, and in the latter case the reflection \(k\mapsto2^{M+1}-1-k\), together with square congruence and bit-complement identities, converts it to exact equality.

full_proof.text:
We prove that for every natural number \(n\) there is a natural number \(k\) such that
\[
 k^2\mathbin{\operatorname{XOR}}(k+1)^2=(2n+1)^2.
\]
Here \(\operatorname{XOR}\) and \(\operatorname{AND}\) are the bitwise operations on nonnegative integers.

We will use the following elementary facts about binary arithmetic.

1. For all nonnegative integers \(a,b\),
\[
 a+b=(a\mathbin{\operatorname{XOR}}b)+2(a\mathbin{\operatorname{AND}}b).
\tag{1}
\]
Indeed, this holds independently in every binary position: XOR records addition without carry, while a position in which both bits are 1 contributes a carry of twice that place value.

2. AND distributes over XOR:
\[
 (a\mathbin{\operatorname{XOR}}b)\mathbin{\operatorname{AND}}c
 = (a\mathbin{\operatorname{AND}}c)\mathbin{\operatorname{XOR}}(b\mathbin{\operatorname{AND}}c).
\tag{2}
\]
This follows by checking the three bits at each binary position.

3. Congruence modulo \(2^t\) means equality of the lowest \(t\) binary bits. Consequently, if
\(x\equiv y\pmod {2^t}\), then
\[
 x\mathbin{\operatorname{AND}}M\equiv y\mathbin{\operatorname{AND}}M\pmod {2^t}.
\tag{3}
\]
In particular, if both AND expressions are less than \(2^t\), this congruence is an equality.

We begin by transforming the equation to be solved. Put
\[
 M=(2n+1)^2,
 \qquad
 N=2n^2+2n.
\]
Expanding the square gives
\[
 M=4n^2+4n+1=2N+1.
\tag{4}
\]
Notice also that \(N\) is even.

We claim that, for every \(k\geq 0\),
\[
 k^2\mathbin{\operatorname{XOR}}(k+1)^2=M
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 k+(k^2\mathbin{\operatorname{AND}}M)=N.
\tag{5}
\]
To see this, write
\[
 x=k^2,\qquad y=(k+1)^2=x+2k+1,
 \qquad c=x\mathbin{\operatorname{AND}}M.
\]
The XOR equation \(x\mathbin{\operatorname{XOR}}y=M\) is equivalent, by XORing both sides with \(x\), to
\[
 x\mathbin{\operatorname{XOR}}M=y.
\tag{6}
\]
Applying (1) to \(x\) and \(M\), and using \(M=2N+1\), gives
\[
 x+2N+1=(x\mathbin{\operatorname{XOR}}M)+2c.
\tag{7}
\]
If (6) holds, then the right side is \(y+2c=x+2k+1+2c\); cancellation in (7) yields \(N=k+c\). Conversely, if \(N=k+c\), then
\[
 x+2N+1=x+2k+2c+1=y+2c.
\]
Comparison with (7), followed by cancellation of \(2c\), yields \(x\mathbin{\operatorname{XOR}}M=y\), which is equivalent to the desired XOR equation. This proves (5).

Thus it suffices to solve
\[
 g(k):=k+(k^2\mathbin{\operatorname{AND}}M)=N.
\tag{8}
\]
We first solve this equation modulo arbitrary powers of two.

Claim. If \(N\) is even, then for every integer \(i\geq 0\) there exists \(k_i\) with
\[
 0\leq k_i<2^i
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 g(k_i)\equiv N\pmod {2^i}.
\tag{9}
\]

We prove the claim by induction on \(i\). For \(i=0\), the modulus is \(1\), so \(k_0=0\) works.

Suppose that \(k<2^i\) has already been found with
\(g(k)\equiv N\pmod {2^i}\). We seek a solution modulo \(2^{i+1}\). If \(g(k)\equiv N\pmod {2^{i+1}}\), we retain \(k\). Otherwise we will use \(k+2^i\).

For \(i\geq 1\), expansion gives
\[
 (k+2^i)^2-k^2=2^{i+1}k+2^{2i},
\]
and both terms on the right are divisible by \(2^{i+1}\). Hence
\[
 (k+2^i)^2\equiv k^2\pmod {2^{i+1}}.
\tag{10}
\]
By (3), AND with \(M\) preserves this congruence. Therefore
\[
 g(k+2^i)
 \equiv g(k)+2^i\pmod {2^{i+1}}.
\tag{11}
\]
There are exactly two residue classes modulo \(2^{i+1}\) above any fixed residue class modulo \(2^i\), and they differ by \(2^i\). Since \(g(k)\) and \(N\) agree modulo \(2^i\), if they do not agree modulo \(2^{i+1}\), adding \(2^i\) to \(g(k)\) makes them agree. Equation (11) then shows that \(k+2^i\) is the required lifted solution. Moreover,
\[
 k+2^i<2^i+2^i=2^{i+1}.
\]

The only point not covered by (10) is the first lift, where \(i=0\). At that stage the only possible old representative is \(k=0\), and
\[
 g(0)=0.
\]
Because \(N\) is even, \(g(0)\equiv N\pmod 2\), so the old representative already works and no shift is needed. This completes the induction and proves the claim.

We now apply (9) with
\[
 w=M+1.
\]
Since \(M<2^w\), and since \(N<M\) by (4), we also have \(N<2^w\). We obtain some \(k_0<2^w\) such that
\[
 g(k_0)\equiv N\pmod {2^w}.
\tag{12}
\]
Set
\[
 c_0=k_0^2\mathbin{\operatorname{AND}}M,
 \qquad
 g_0=k_0+c_0.
\]
Every 1-bit of \(c_0\) is a 1-bit of \(M\), so
\[
 0\leq c_0\leq M<2^w.
\tag{13}
\]
Together with \(k_0<2^w\), this gives
\[
 0\leq g_0<2^{w+1}.
\tag{14}
\]
On the other hand, (12) says that \(g_0\equiv N\pmod {2^w}\), with \(0\leq N<2^w\). There are only two numbers below \(2^{w+1}\) having this residue modulo \(2^w\). Thus
\[
 g_0=N
 \quad\text{or}\quad
 g_0=N+2^w.
\tag{15}
\]

In the first case, (8) is solved by \(k_0\), and (5) immediately gives
\[
 k_0^2\mathbin{\operatorname{XOR}}(k_0+1)^2=M.
\]
It remains to handle the second, overflow case. Assume therefore that
\[
 k_0+c_0=N+2^w.
\tag{16}
\]
We will replace \(k_0\) by its complement below \(2^w\):
\[
 k_1=2^w-1-k_0.
\tag{17}
\]
This is a nonnegative integer because \(k_0<2^w\), and it satisfies
\[
 k_1+(k_0+1)=2^w.
\tag{18}
\]
We next determine \(k_1^2\mathbin{\operatorname{AND}}M\).

First, let \(x=k_0^2\). The carry identity (1) says
\[
 x+M=(x\mathbin{\operatorname{XOR}}M)+2c_0.
\tag{19}
\]
Using \(M=2N+1\) and the overflow relation (16), we calculate
\[
\begin{aligned}
 (k_0+1)^2+2c_0
 &=x+2k_0+1+2c_0\\
 &=x+2(k_0+c_0)+1\\
 &=x+2N+2^{w+1}+1\\
 &=x+M+2^{w+1}\\
 &=(x\mathbin{\operatorname{XOR}}M)+2c_0+2^{w+1},
\end{aligned}
\]
where the final equality uses (19). Cancelling \(2c_0\) gives
\[
 (k_0+1)^2=(k_0^2\mathbin{\operatorname{XOR}}M)+2^{w+1}.
\tag{20}
\]
In particular,
\[
 (k_0+1)^2\equiv k_0^2\mathbin{\operatorname{XOR}}M\pmod {2^w}.
\tag{21}
\]
ANDing both sides with \(M\) preserves the low \(w\) bits. Moreover, each resulting AND is at most \(M<2^w\), so congruence modulo \(2^w\) implies actual equality. Hence
\[
 (k_0+1)^2\mathbin{\operatorname{AND}}M
 = (k_0^2\mathbin{\operatorname{XOR}}M)\mathbin{\operatorname{AND}}M.
\tag{22}
\]
Using distributivity (2) and \(M\mathbin{\operatorname{AND}}M=M\), the right side is
\[
 (k_0^2\mathbin{\operatorname{AND}}M)
 \mathbin{\operatorname{XOR}}M
 =c_0\mathbin{\operatorname{XOR}}M.
\]
Thus
\[
 (k_0+1)^2\mathbin{\operatorname{AND}}M=c_0\mathbin{\operatorname{XOR}}M.
\tag{23}
\]

Next, (18) gives \(k_1\equiv -(k_0+1)\pmod {2^w}\), so squaring yields
\[
 k_1^2\equiv (k_0+1)^2\pmod {2^w}.
\tag{24}
\]
After ANDing with \(M\), both resulting numbers are at most \(M<2^w\), so they are equal. Combining this with (23), we obtain
\[
 k_1^2\mathbin{\operatorname{AND}}M=c_0\mathbin{\operatorname{XOR}}M.
\tag{25}
\]

Because \(c_0=k_0^2\mathbin{\operatorname{AND}}M\), every 1-bit of \(c_0\) occurs among the 1-bits of \(M\). Thus \(c_0\mathbin{\operatorname{XOR}}M\) consists precisely of the remaining 1-bits of \(M\), and the two numbers have no common 1-bit. Consequently their ordinary sum is \(M\):
\[
 c_0+(c_0\mathbin{\operatorname{XOR}}M)=M.
\tag{26}
\]
We may now evaluate \(g(k_1)\). From (17), (25), and (26),
\[
\begin{aligned}
 g(k_1)
 &=k_1+(k_1^2\mathbin{\operatorname{AND}}M)\\
 &=2^w-1-k_0+(c_0\mathbin{\operatorname{XOR}}M)\\
 &=2^w-1-k_0+(M-c_0)\\
 &=2^w-1+M-(k_0+c_0).
\end{aligned}
\]
Using (16), this becomes
\[
 g(k_1)=2^w-1+M-(N+2^w)=M-N-1.
\]
Finally, \(M=2N+1\), so
\[
 g(k_1)=N.
\tag{27}
\]
Thus the additive equation (8) is solved by \(k_1\) in the overflow case as well. Applying the equivalence (5) once more gives
\[
 k_1^2\mathbin{\operatorname{XOR}}(k_1+1)^2=M=(2n+1)^2.
\]

We have therefore produced a suitable natural number \(k\) for every \(n\geq 0\). Hence the set from which the least value in A224515 is chosen is always nonempty, so the sequence never takes the fallback value \(-1\); equivalently, \(a(n)\geq 0\) for every \(n\geq 0\).
